1.modern-en: Elinor tries to steady her mother’s grief and anger after Henry Dashwood’s death. Her judgment gives her influence in the family despite her youth.
1.original-en: Elinor tries to steady her mother’s grief and anger after Henry Dashwood’s death. Her judgment gives her influence in the family despite her youth.

3.modern-en: Elinor finds much to value in Edward Ferrars’s understanding and kindness, though Marianne is disappointed by his reading aloud.
3.original-en: Elinor finds much to value in Edward Ferrars’s understanding and kindness, though Marianne is disappointed by his reading aloud.

4.modern-en: Elinor defends Edward to Marianne but refuses to assume that his affection will lead to marriage. Fanny’s pointed remarks about his family’s expectations help drive Mrs. Dashwood to accept the cottage at Barton.
4.original-en: Elinor defends Edward to Marianne but refuses to assume that his affection will lead to marriage. Fanny’s pointed remarks about his family’s expectations help drive Mrs. Dashwood to accept the cottage at Barton.

5.modern-en: Elinor leaves Norland with her mother and sisters. Edward is invited to visit them, while John’s promised assistance remains unfulfilled.
5.original-en: Elinor leaves Norland with her mother and sisters. Edward is invited to visit them, while John’s promised assistance remains unfulfilled.

6.modern-en: Elinor settles with her family at Barton Cottage. Visits from Sir John and Lady Middleton introduce the household to its new neighbours.
6.original-en: Elinor settles with her family at Barton Cottage. Visits from Sir John and Lady Middleton introduce the household to its new neighbours.

7.modern-en: Elinor joins the family’s dinner at Barton Park, where Mrs. Jennings jokes about the sisters’ possible attachments and Colonel Brandon listens attentively to Marianne’s music.
7.original-en: Elinor joins the family’s dinner at Barton Park, where Mrs. Jennings jokes about the sisters’ possible attachments and Colonel Brandon listens attentively to Marianne’s music.

8.modern-en: Elinor challenges Marianne’s dismissal of Colonel Brandon as too old for love. Marianne also finds the restrained behaviour of Elinor and Edward difficult to understand.
8.original-en: Elinor challenges Marianne’s dismissal of Colonel Brandon as too old for love. Marianne also finds the restrained behaviour of Elinor and Edward difficult to understand.

9.modern-en: Elinor asks Sir John about Willoughby after he carries the injured Marianne home. Sir John turns his account of the young man into teasing advice about catching a husband.
9.original-en: Elinor asks Sir John about Willoughby after he carries the injured Marianne home. Sir John turns his account of the young man into teasing advice about catching a husband.

10.modern-en: Elinor observes how quickly Marianne and Willoughby agree in their tastes. She defends Colonel Brandon when the two speak slightingly of him.
10.original-en: Elinor observes how quickly Marianne and Willoughby agree in their tastes. She defends Colonel Brandon when the two speak slightingly of him.

11.modern-en: Elinor finds Colonel Brandon a companion worth talking to while Marianne and Willoughby increasingly withdraw into each other’s company. His remarks suggest an earlier acquaintance with feelings like Marianne’s.
11.original-en: Elinor finds Colonel Brandon a companion worth talking to while Marianne and Willoughby increasingly withdraw into each other’s company. His remarks suggest an earlier acquaintance with feelings like Marianne’s.

12.modern-en: Elinor persuades Marianne to refuse Willoughby’s gift of a horse because keeping it would burden their mother. Margaret’s account of a lock of hair strengthens her suspicion of an engagement.
12.original-en: Elinor persuades Marianne to refuse Willoughby’s gift of a horse because keeping it would burden their mother. Margaret’s account of a lock of hair strengthens her suspicion of an engagement.

13.modern-en: Elinor questions Marianne about visiting Allenham with Willoughby while Mrs. Smith was at home. Marianne regards the visit very differently from her sister.
13.original-en: Elinor questions Marianne about visiting Allenham with Willoughby while Mrs. Smith was at home. Marianne regards the visit very differently from her sister.

14.modern-en: Elinor and her mother differ over whether Marianne and Willoughby are engaged. Elinor wants clearer evidence; Mrs. Dashwood trusts their visible attachment.
14.original-en: Elinor and her mother differ over whether Marianne and Willoughby are engaged. Elinor wants clearer evidence; Mrs. Dashwood trusts their visible attachment.

15.modern-en: Elinor finds Willoughby’s abrupt departure and refusal of an invitation to return difficult to explain. Her mother supplies hopeful explanations while Marianne gives way to grief.
15.original-en: Elinor finds Willoughby’s abrupt departure and refusal of an invitation to return difficult to explain. Her mother supplies hopeful explanations while Marianne gives way to grief.

16.modern-en: Elinor encounters Edward during a walk with Marianne. His arrival pleases her, but his manner gives little of the reassurance she wants.
16.original-en: Elinor encounters Edward during a walk with Marianne. His arrival pleases her, but his manner gives little of the reassurance she wants.

17.modern-en: Elinor hears Edward discuss his limited ambitions and his family’s expectations. Conversation about money and happiness exposes differences among the visitors and their hosts.
17.original-en: Elinor hears Edward discuss his limited ambitions and his family’s expectations. Conversation about money and happiness exposes differences among the visitors and their hosts.

18.modern-en: Elinor notices a ring containing hair on Edward’s hand and privately believes the hair to be her own. His subdued behaviour continues to trouble her.
18.original-en: Elinor notices a ring containing hair on Edward’s hand and privately believes the hair to be her own. His subdued behaviour continues to trouble her.

19.modern-en: Elinor is hurt by Edward’s departure but keeps herself occupied instead of displaying her distress. The arrival of the Palmers brings fresh company to Barton.
19.original-en: Elinor is hurt by Edward’s departure but keeps herself occupied instead of displaying her distress. The arrival of the Palmers brings fresh company to Barton.

20.modern-en: Elinor listens to Mrs. Palmer’s cheerful accounts of her husband and acquaintances, finding contradictions in what she says about Colonel Brandon.
20.original-en: Elinor listens to Mrs. Palmer’s cheerful accounts of her husband and acquaintances, finding contradictions in what she says about Colonel Brandon.

21.modern-en: Elinor meets the Steele sisters and dislikes their flattery and intrusive questions. Their apparent acquaintance with Edward draws her attention.
21.original-en: Elinor meets the Steele sisters and dislikes their flattery and intrusive questions. Their apparent acquaintance with Edward draws her attention.

22.modern-en: Lucy tells Elinor that she has been secretly engaged to Edward for four years. Elinor controls her reaction while a miniature, a letter and the account of the hair ring supply painful evidence.
22.original-en: Lucy tells Elinor that she has been secretly engaged to Edward for four years. Elinor controls her reaction while a miniature, a letter and the account of the hair ring supply painful evidence.

23.modern-en: Elinor accepts the truth of Lucy’s disclosure and believes Edward’s attachment to Lucy has changed. Unable to confide in her family, she arranges an opportunity to speak to Lucy again.
23.original-en: Elinor accepts the truth of Lucy’s disclosure and believes Edward’s attachment to Lucy has changed. Unable to confide in her family, she arranges an opportunity to speak to Lucy again.

24.modern-en: Elinor questions Lucy about the engagement without revealing her own feelings. Lucy seeks reassurance and advice while watching closely for signs of a rival.
24.original-en: Elinor questions Lucy about the engagement without revealing her own feelings. Lucy seeks reassurance and advice while watching closely for signs of a rival.

25.modern-en: Elinor reluctantly agrees to accompany Marianne to London under Mrs. Jennings’s care. Marianne hopes the visit will bring her to Willoughby.
25.original-en: Elinor reluctantly agrees to accompany Marianne to London under Mrs. Jennings’s care. Marianne hopes the visit will bring her to Willoughby.

26.modern-en: Elinor watches Marianne eagerly send a letter and wait for a visitor who does not come. Colonel Brandon calls, but Marianne’s hopes are fixed elsewhere.
26.original-en: Elinor watches Marianne eagerly send a letter and wait for a visitor who does not come. Colonel Brandon calls, but Marianne’s hopes are fixed elsewhere.

27.modern-en: Elinor writes to her mother about Marianne’s anxiety. Brandon, believing Marianne engaged to Willoughby, speaks to Elinor about the attachment.
27.original-en: Elinor writes to her mother about Marianne’s anxiety. Brandon, believing Marianne engaged to Willoughby, speaks to Elinor about the attachment.

28.modern-en: Elinor witnesses Willoughby’s cold reception of Marianne at an evening party. She tries to restrain and comfort her sister after the encounter.
28.original-en: Elinor witnesses Willoughby’s cold reception of Marianne at an evening party. She tries to restrain and comfort her sister after the encounter.

29.modern-en: Elinor reads Willoughby’s letter returning Marianne’s letters and lock of hair. Marianne tells her that there was no formal engagement, though she believed their affection unmistakable.
29.original-en: Elinor reads Willoughby’s letter returning Marianne’s letters and lock of hair. Marianne tells her that there was no formal engagement, though she believed their affection unmistakable.

30.modern-en: Elinor hears Mrs. Jennings’s news of Willoughby’s wealthy intended bride. Brandon learns from Elinor that the supposed engagement to Marianne never existed.
30.original-en: Elinor hears Mrs. Jennings’s news of Willoughby’s wealthy intended bride. Brandon learns from Elinor that the supposed engagement to Marianne never existed.

31.modern-en: Elinor listens to Brandon’s history of the two Elizas and his account of Willoughby’s treatment of his ward. The disclosure changes what she can tell Marianne about him.
31.original-en: Elinor listens to Brandon’s history of the two Elizas and his account of Willoughby’s treatment of his ward. The disclosure changes what she can tell Marianne about him.

32.modern-en: Elinor repeats Brandon’s account to Marianne. She also has to endure Lucy’s renewed confidences and the Steele sisters’ intrusive visit.
32.original-en: Elinor repeats Brandon’s account to Marianne. She also has to endure Lucy’s renewed confidences and the Steele sisters’ intrusive visit.

33.modern-en: Elinor meets John Dashwood in London and introduces him to Colonel Brandon. John speculates about Brandon’s income and an advantageous marriage for her.
33.original-en: Elinor meets John Dashwood in London and introduces him to Colonel Brandon. John speculates about Brandon’s income and an advantageous marriage for her.

34.modern-en: Elinor meets Mrs. Ferrars at a dinner given by John and Fanny. Mrs. Ferrars favours Lucy and treats Elinor coldly, provoking Marianne to defend her sister.
34.original-en: Elinor meets Mrs. Ferrars at a dinner given by John and Fanny. Mrs. Ferrars favours Lucy and treats Elinor coldly, provoking Marianne to defend her sister.

35.modern-en: Elinor endures Lucy’s triumph over Mrs. Ferrars’s reception. Edward’s unexpected visit leaves the three painfully constrained, while Marianne misunderstands their situation.
35.original-en: Elinor endures Lucy’s triumph over Mrs. Ferrars’s reception. Edward’s unexpected visit leaves the three painfully constrained, while Marianne misunderstands their situation.

36.modern-en: Elinor attends a musical party with Fanny and hears Robert Ferrars discuss cottages and his own opinions. Fanny arranges to invite the Steele sisters to stay.
36.original-en: Elinor attends a musical party with Fanny and hears Robert Ferrars discuss cottages and his own opinions. Fanny arranges to invite the Steele sisters to stay.

37.modern-en: Elinor learns that Lucy’s engagement has become known to Fanny and Mrs. Ferrars. She tells Marianne how long she has carried the secret, and hears that Edward has refused to abandon Lucy despite losing his mother’s financial support.
37.original-en: Elinor learns that Lucy’s engagement has become known to Fanny and Mrs. Ferrars. She tells Marianne how long she has carried the secret, and hears that Edward has refused to abandon Lucy despite losing his mother’s financial support.

38.modern-en: Elinor hears Anne Steele’s account of Edward and Lucy’s meeting, then rebukes her for listening at the door. Lucy’s letter presents the couple’s situation in a more carefully managed light.
38.original-en: Elinor hears Anne Steele’s account of Edward and Lucy’s meeting, then rebukes her for listening at the door. Lucy’s letter presents the couple’s situation in a more carefully managed light.

39.modern-en: Elinor agrees to tell Edward that Colonel Brandon is offering him the living at Delaford. Brandon explains that its income is small, though it will allow Edward to enter the church.
39.original-en: Elinor agrees to tell Edward that Colonel Brandon is offering him the living at Delaford. Brandon explains that its income is small, though it will allow Edward to enter the church.

40.modern-en: Elinor clears up Mrs. Jennings’s mistaken belief that Brandon has proposed to her. She tells Edward about the living and insists that the kindness is Brandon’s.
40.original-en: Elinor clears up Mrs. Jennings’s mistaken belief that Brandon has proposed to her. She tells Edward about the living and insists that the kindness is Brandon’s.

41.modern-en: Elinor hears John’s astonishment at Brandon giving away the living. Robert speaks dismissively of Edward’s choice and prospects.
41.original-en: Elinor hears John’s astonishment at Brandon giving away the living. Robert speaks dismissively of Edward’s choice and prospects.

42.modern-en: Elinor travels to Cleveland with Marianne and the Palmers. Brandon speaks with her about Edward’s parsonage, while Marianne’s long damp walks bring on a cold.
42.original-en: Elinor travels to Cleveland with Marianne and the Palmers. Brandon speaks with her about Edward’s parsonage, while Marianne’s long damp walks bring on a cold.

43.modern-en: Elinor nurses Marianne as her illness becomes dangerous. Brandon leaves to fetch their mother; when a carriage arrives, Elinor discovers Willoughby instead.
43.original-en: Elinor nurses Marianne as her illness becomes dangerous. Brandon leaves to fetch their mother; when a carriage arrives, Elinor discovers Willoughby instead.

44.modern-en: Elinor hears Willoughby’s account of his conduct towards Marianne, Eliza and his wife. His distress moves her without removing the wrong he has done.
44.original-en: Elinor hears Willoughby’s account of his conduct towards Marianne, Eliza and his wife. His distress moves her without removing the wrong he has done.

45.modern-en: Elinor reflects uneasily on Willoughby’s confession. Her mother arrives, finds Marianne recovering, and tells Elinor of Brandon’s attachment to Marianne.
45.original-en: Elinor reflects uneasily on Willoughby’s confession. Her mother arrives, finds Marianne recovering, and tells Elinor of Brandon’s attachment to Marianne.

46.modern-en: Back at Barton, Elinor listens as Marianne examines her past behaviour and describes a different way of living. She then tells Marianne what Willoughby said at Cleveland.
46.original-en: Back at Barton, Elinor listens as Marianne examines her past behaviour and describes a different way of living. She then tells Marianne what Willoughby said at Cleveland.

47.modern-en: Elinor and her mother consider Willoughby’s explanation. A servant’s report that Mr. Ferrars has married Lucy convinces them that Edward is lost to Elinor.
47.original-en: Elinor and her mother consider Willoughby’s explanation. A servant’s report that Mr. Ferrars has married Lucy convinces them that Edward is lost to Elinor.

48.modern-en: Edward arrives at Barton and explains that Lucy has married Robert. Elinor leaves the room in tears when she understands that Edward is free.
48.original-en: Edward arrives at Barton and explains that Lucy has married Robert. Elinor leaves the room in tears when she understands that Edward is free.

49.modern-en: Elinor accepts Edward’s proposal. They discuss his former engagement and Lucy’s marriage, while letters bring news of the Ferrars family’s reaction.
49.original-en: Elinor accepts Edward’s proposal. They discuss his former engagement and Lucy’s marriage, while letters bring news of the Ferrars family’s reaction.

50.modern-en: Elinor and Edward marry and settle at Delaford after Mrs. Ferrars provides additional money. The sisters’ households remain closely connected when Marianne marries Brandon.
50.original-en: Elinor and Edward marry and settle at Delaford after Mrs. Ferrars provides additional money. The sisters’ households remain closely connected when Marianne marries Brandon.

1.original-en: Marianne shares her mother’s unrestrained grief, while Elinor worries about the excess of her feelings.

3.original-en: Marianne finds Edward’s reading aloud insufficiently expressive and doubts that he can satisfy Elinor’s taste.

8.original-en: Marianne dismisses the idea of Colonel Brandon as a lover because of his age. She also wonders why Edward and Elinor show so little outward agitation at parting.

9.original-en: Marianne falls and twists her ankle during a walk. Willoughby carries her home, making an immediate impression on her and her mother.

10.modern-en: Marianne discovers that Willoughby shares her tastes in books, music and dancing. Their agreement encourages an unusually rapid intimacy.
10.original-en: Marianne discovers that Willoughby shares her tastes in books, music and dancing. Their agreement encourages an unusually rapid intimacy.

12.original-en: Marianne wants to accept a horse from Willoughby but yields to Elinor’s objections about its expense. Margaret reports seeing him take a lock of Marianne’s hair.

13.original-en: Marianne visits Allenham with Willoughby and describes the house enthusiastically. She resists Elinor’s criticism of entering it without knowing Mrs. Smith.

15.original-en: Marianne is overwhelmed by Willoughby’s sudden departure for London and cannot explain it to her family.

16.original-en: Marianne deliberately dwells on her grief for Willoughby. On a walk she briefly mistakes an approaching rider for him, before recognising Edward.

25.modern-en: Marianne eagerly accepts Mrs. Jennings’s invitation to London, hoping to see Willoughby.

26.modern-en: Marianne sends a letter soon after arriving in London and waits impatiently for Willoughby. Brandon’s arrival disappoints her.
26.original-en: Marianne sends a letter soon after arriving in London and waits impatiently for Willoughby. Brandon’s arrival disappoints her.

27.original-en: Marianne continues to wait for a reply and becomes increasingly distressed by Willoughby’s absence.

28.modern-en: Marianne approaches Willoughby at a party and is met with cold formality. She cannot reconcile his conduct with their intimacy at Barton.
28.original-en: Marianne approaches Willoughby at a party and is met with cold formality. She cannot reconcile his conduct with their intimacy at Barton.

29.modern-en: Marianne receives Willoughby’s letter denying any attachment and returning her letters and hair. She tells Elinor that they had never been formally engaged.
29.original-en: Marianne receives Willoughby’s letter denying any attachment and returning her letters and hair. She tells Elinor that they had never been formally engaged.

35.original-en: Marianne welcomes Edward warmly, unaware of his engagement to Lucy, and mistakes Elinor’s constrained behaviour.

46.original-en: Marianne returns to Barton and reflects critically on her behaviour. She asks Elinor to tell her about Willoughby’s visit.
